lesson.title: Eisenhower's Warning: Peace, Power, and the Military-Industrial Complex
lesson.summary: Dwight Eisenhower ended the Korean War and presided over a peacetime defense buildup so large that in his final speech as president he warned Americans about the very system he had helped create.
lesson.body:
Dwight D. Eisenhower came to the presidency in 1953 as the most famous soldier in America, the general who had commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II. One of his first acts in office was to help bring the Korean War to a close. Fighting had dragged on since 1950 between North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, and South Korea, backed by the United States and United Nations forces, and in July 1953 an armistice was signed at Panmunjom that stopped the fighting, though it left Korea divided near the same border where the war had started and never formally ended the conflict with a full peace treaty.

Even with the shooting war over, the Cold War did not relax. The Soviet Union remained a nuclear armed rival, and Eisenhower, despite being a career military man, worried about the cost of a permanent arms race. His administration adopted a strategy sometimes called the New Look, which leaned on nuclear weapons and airpower as a cheaper way to deter the Soviets than maintaining huge standing armies. Paradoxically, this approach still required enormous, continuous spending on missiles, bombers, and warheads, developed and built by a growing web of private defense contractors working under government contract.

That web grew larger still after October 1957, when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth. Sputnik shocked Americans, who had assumed U.S. technology led the world, and it triggered fears that the Soviets might also lead in missile technology. The federal government responded with new spending on science, education, and rockets, and in 1958 created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, known as NASA, formally launching the Space Race between the two superpowers, a contest that would eventually reach the moon in the following decade.

By the end of his presidency, Eisenhower had watched defense spending, nuclear stockpiles, and the industries that supplied them grow into a permanent and enormously influential part of the American economy and government, something that had never existed in peacetime before World War II. In his farewell address on January 17, 1961, he coined a phrase that has outlived almost everything else he said in office: he warned the nation to guard against the unwarranted influence of what he called the military industrial complex, the close alliance between the armed forces, weapons manufacturers, and the members of Congress who funded them. It was a striking admission from the man who had led that buildup for eight years, and it reflected his genuine worry that a democracy could lose control over its own priorities if military spending became too politically entrenched to question.
